question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 1 \\ -15 & -1 & -15 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a & ∗ \\ 0 & b & ∗ \\ 1 & c & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $a+c.$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ may be written as a composition of Jordan blocks, as follows:

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-1)
$$

So, we have

- a single $2\times 2$ Jordan block corresponding to $\lambda =4,$ and

- a single $1\times 1$ block corresponding to $\lambda =-1.$

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(4) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(-1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A+I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =4,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-4I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 1 \\ -15 & -1 & -15 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -15 & -5 & -15 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-4I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -15 & -5 & -15 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+15{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & -15 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the first and second equation, we have ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}-1$ and ${x}_{2}=3,$ respectively.

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3}-1 \\ 3 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a+c=-1+0=-1.$
